\[
R_\sigma(x) = D_{xx}(x)\, D_{yy}(x) - 0.81\, D_{xy}(x)^2,
\qquad
(x, \sigma) \text{ is a blob if } R_\sigma(x) = \max_{3 \times 3 \times 3} R \ge T,
\qquad
r \approx \sigma,\quad T = 0.01
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(D_{xx}, D_{yy}, D_{xy}\): Box-filter second derivatives at scale sigma
- \(r\): The radius of the blob
- \(T\): The threshold

The Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives. At the middle of a blob, both curvatures have the same sign, so its determinant is large and positive. Bay and coworkers replaced the Gaussian second derivatives by box filters that the integral image sums in constant time, so every scale costs the same. Here scikit-image uses boxes that span floor(3 sigma) pixels and divides each sum by the square of that size. It weights the mixed term by 0.81 = 0.9^2, as SURF does. For true second derivatives, a negated image has the same determinant, so bright and dark blobs are both found. The boxes of scikit-image only sum to zero when floor(3 sigma) is a multiple of 3, so the brightness level itself also adds a little to the response. On the negated Disks image, the same blobs come out with slightly different sizes and scores, and one more appears in a corner. Peaks over position and scale above the threshold are blobs, and overlapping blobs are pruned. The radius is about sigma. The score is R at the peak.
